title: The Hens' Own Plan
part: PART FOUR: THE OTHER KIND OF CONFIDENCE

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #45: Try to be somebody else's team.*

The yellow bus hums, a low vibration that travels up through the vinyl seats and into my bones. The windows are down, letting in the smell of diesel and the sharp, green scent of the depot grass. I am sitting in the middle row. I am not wearing the yellow armband. It sits on the seat next to me, folded neatly like a piece of toast.

Coach Gin stands at the front, holding a whiteboard marker like a sword. "Dani," she says, not looking up from her notes. "You are here. That is good. But the armband is not mine to give out. It belongs to the team. So we will decide."

The team is silent. Priya’s hands are in her lap. Tank looks at his shoes. Josie opens her mouth, then closes it.

"Vote," Gin says. "Socks. One sock, one vote. Throw them into the bin."

Nobody moves. Then, one by one, they toss their socks into the plastic bin. They land in a soft, white pile. The armband is placed on the pile. It is back on my arm, but this time, it feels heavier. It feels earned.
pages.image: A group of children sitting inside a big blank yellow minibus with windows down, looking at a yellow armband resting on a pile of white socks in a bin, a woman in a yellow jacket holding a marker, bright daylight.

pages.text:
Gin writes the word GOOD on the whiteboard in big, block letters, then taps it with the marker to get our attention.

"Everyone," she says, her voice flat and steady, "tell me what you are good at. Not what you want to be. What you actually do."

Tank clears his throat, which sounds like a truck shifting gears. "Standing in the right place," he says quietly. "Most of the time."

Josie raises her hand so fast it blurs. "Seeing what's happening and saying it out loud so everyone knows."

Leo and Mateo speak at the same time, their voices merging into one loud echo. "Making noise on the left."

Ahmed shrugs, looking bored by his own greatness. "Going fast. And, apparently, passing."

Priya looks down at her oversized gloves, fiddling with the velcro. "Angles," she whispers, barely audible. "I see where they are going."

Ollie grins, holding up an orange slice he has been saving. "Everybody else. I keep everyone happy."

They all look at me. The marker squeaks against the whiteboard. I take the pen from Gin and write the last word, my hand steady for once. "Seeing where it's going."

The board is full now. It is not a list of skills. It is a map.
pages.image: A blank white easel board with scribbled arrows with the word GOOD written on it, a group of diverse children looking at it, a girl with a ponytail writing on the board, a boy in a green shirt, a girl with glasses, a large boy, and a small boy holding orange slices.

pages.text:
The plan is simple. We do not fight the slope. We use it.

"The field slants left," Gin says, drawing a line on the board. "So we push the ball to the left, let the slope carry it, and we wait for it to come back."

Ahmed stays high and fast, ready to chase. The twins hold the left side, using a hand signal to switch positions. Priya calls the angles from her net, her voice clear and calm. Josie’s commentary is now a job title: Voice. She narrates the flow, keeping us honest.

Ollie will come on for the last ten minutes. He brings orange slices. He brings energy. He is the secret weapon we did not know we needed.

It is not fancy. It is not pretty. It is exactly what we are.
pages.image: A diagram of a slanted soccer field with arrows showing the ball moving left and right, a group of children standing around a blank white easel board with scribbled arrows, a girl with a ponytail pointing at the diagram, a boy with a high ponytail, a girl with glasses, and a large boy.

pages.text:
We practice until the sun drops low and the shadows stretch long across the grass. The first attempt is a disaster. The ball rolls left, straight into the duck pond. A single mallard floats by, staring at the sunken ball with the expression of a principal watching a student chew gum in class.

Gin takes a sip from her thermos. "Excellent data," she says.

The third attempt is better. We pass the ball through four players. Ahmed makes a pass that is not fast, but it is there. The ball hits the post and bounces back into the net.

Nobody cheers. We do not run and hug. We just look at each other. There is a quiet understanding in the air. We did not win a game. We did something harder. We played together.
pages.image: A soccer ball hitting the crossbar and bouncing into the net, a group of children standing still and looking at each other, a muddy field with a duck pond in the background, low golden sunlight, a girl with a ponytail, a boy in a green shirt, and a girl with glasses.

pages.text:
The sun is dropping behind the hills, painting the sky in shades of bruised purple and orange. The air feels cool against my scraped knees, a nice change from the heavy heat of the practice field. My legs ache, but it is the good kind of pain, the kind that means I actually did something with them today. I have had a whole afternoon behind me, and for the first time in forever, I do not have a single stat to worry about.

I stop at the corner of Maple and 4th Street and check my sock. The card is there. It is just a card. It does not need to be anything else. It is not a trophy, and it is not a promise. It is just a piece of paper with my name on it, tucked safely away where the scoreboard cannot reach.

Saturday is coming. The Northgate Wolves are coming. They are loud, they are polished, and they have never lost a game. But I am not afraid. Whatever the score ends up being, it cannot take the card out of my sock. It cannot change the fact that I am Dani Ruiz, I am the captain, and I am good.
pages.image: A girl with a high ponytail and a yellow armband walking home on a dirt path, looking at the setting sun, a muddy soccer field in the distance, a calm and peaceful mood, a small duck in a pond nearby.
